title: Schefter Learned to Point at Things
summary: Every Schefter post now links to the thing it is about — columns, transactions, rumors, trade speculation — and works in the tool that answers whatever question the paragraph just raised. His schedule release article somehow never linked to the schedule release page.
description: Claude Schefter filed eight paragraphs about the 2026 schedule — the four games to circle, the rivalry records, the bye-week math — and never once told you where to go read the thing. The schedule release page was right there. The column existed to announce it. Not a link in sight.

It turned out not to be a slip in one article. Searching every feed for a link — 762 posts across both leagues, every kind of thing he files — turned up almost nothing. He had never linked to anything from a column. Nineteen transaction cards in a row reported a player getting dropped without offering a way to go claim him. Two posts floated a hypothetical trade, named both teams and both players, and gave you nothing to click.

Now every article declares where it points before a word is written. Go back and read the 2026 schedule release: the opening line is the link, Throwback Week goes to your throwback settings, the rivalry section goes to the rivalry pages, and the closer hands you the full week-by-week grid. The three cut-watch columns from August got the same treatment — over-the-limit rosters, dead weight, a bloated receiver room that the trade builder has opinions about.

The short posts got it too, and they follow what you can actually do about the news. A player dropped is a player anyone reading can claim, so those cards go to the free agent board. A pickup or a trade goes to the rosters. And the trade-speculation posts — the ones that float a deal nobody has actually proposed — now open the Trade Builder with the whole hypothetical already loaded: both teams, both sides of the swap, ready for you to prove Schefter wrong.

The second half of the job is new: Schefter is now expected to plug the site. Not with a paragraph of housekeeping bolted to the end — with the tool that answers the question he just raised. Grading your auction and pointing at the salary benchmarks. Naming the guy you're about to lose and pointing at the free agent board. He picks the ones that fit the story and skips the rest, because a plug he had to wedge in reads like an ad, and nobody clicks a columnist who sounds like an ad.

Two quieter fixes came out of the same sweep. The rumor mill's "Open in Trade Builder" button was sending AFL owners to an empty builder — it was using a parameter only The League's builder reads, so nothing was ever pre-loaded. And when Schefter is required to keep a team anonymous, the button underneath now has to keep the secret too: a rumor that says "a team in the AL East" can no longer carry a link that quietly names which one.

Links he makes up don't survive either. He writes from a list of real pages, and anything that isn't on it gets quietly unwrapped before publishing — the sentence still reads, it just stops promising a page that doesn't exist. And if he forgets the main link entirely, the way he did in August, it gets put back in for him.
imageAlt: The 2026 schedule release article on The Schefter Report, headlined “The 2026 Schedule Is Here. Four Games Will Define It.” under Claude Schefter’s byline. Three phrases in the prose are blue underlined links: “The 2026 schedule for The League is official” in the opening line, “Throwback Week” inside the Week 4 paragraph about Bring the Pain at Vitside Mafia, and “The rivalry renewals are stacked this season” opening the rivalry section.

title: Schedule Release Day Is a Real Day Now
summary: Both leagues get an annual Schedule Release Day — a countdown page that hits zero, locks one schedule for everybody, and puts four games on the board worth circling, rivalry records and all. Same draw for every owner, no reshuffles.
description: The NFL turns its schedule release into a two-hour prime-time special. We used to do ours by way of a commissioner quietly saving a form in May and somebody noticing in August. That is over. Both leagues now have a Schedule Release Day on the calendar, with a page that counts down to it — find it under Offseason War Room in the menu. The League goes June 1; the AFL goes the Sunday two weeks before the National League draft, a date that moves with Labor Day every year, same as the draft it is pinned to.

Open the page before the day and there is a clock — days, hours, minutes, seconds. When it hits zero the schedule locks, and locked is the whole point. The draw is built by an optimizer that could produce a hundred different valid seasons, so if everyone hit a button and got their own, fifteen of sixteen owners would be studying a year that never happens. One schedule gets locked, everybody sees that one, and the copy-and-paste block the commissioner sends to MFL is the exact same one on your screen.

The first thing you get is the tease: four games, four different weeks, each one wearing both franchises’ colors and crests and a line saying why it is there. And the why is not just this year’s records — it is the whole history. The League’s 2026 board opens on a division game in a Week 1 doubleheader, runs the championship rematch in Week 9, and closes in Week 14 with a division title on the line. Records come straight off the same rivalry math the Rivalries pages use, and where the archives disagree with themselves about a pairing — which happens for eighteen of them, a leftover from a franchise identity that changed slots years ago — the card simply says nothing rather than pick a number.

Week 4 gets its own reserved slot, because Week 4 is Throwback Week. The card shows that game the way it will actually be played — old logos, old names, old colors — and the schedule picks it by rivalry rather than by record, so it is the oldest, closest series in the week rather than whoever happens to be good. In 2026 that is Bring the Pain at a Vitside Mafia playing as BOYZ II MEN: fifteen meetings, separated by exactly one game.

Under the tease, the receipts. The schedule is not a shuffle — it is optimized against the constitution and against the NFL’s bye calendar, and the page shows how it did. The League’s 2026 season: 144 games, doubleheaders in Weeks 1, 2, 3 and 12, 40 of a possible 48 division games played on weeks with no NFL byes, and every team with nine home games and nine road games. No more losing a division game because four of your starters were on vacation that Sunday.

Then the full week-by-week grid, so you can find your own season without waiting for MFL to catch up. Any signed-in owner can see all of it. The paste block is commissioner-only, for the obvious reason that saving it in MFL overwrites the entire schedule and there is no undo. And when the paste does land, Claude Schefter files the release column — four games, the rivalries the draw renews, and the records to go with them — and drops it in the chat.
imageAlt: The Schedule Release page reading “The Schedule Is Out — Released Monday, June 1, 2026”, above a Circle These row of four marquee cards. Each is striped with the two franchises’ brand colors and stacks the away team over the home team with their crests. Week 1 Da Dangsters at Pacific Pigskins, tagged division rivalry, opening week and doubleheader week; Week 4 carries a THROWBACK badge and shows old-school logos for Bring The Pain and BOYZ II MEN, labelled Vitside Mafia underneath, tagged “15 meetings, Vitside Mafia up 8-7”; Week 9 Computer Jocks at Dark Magicians of Chaos, tagged championship rematch; Week 14 Running down the Dream at Wascawy Wabbits with a division title on the line. Below sit stat tiles reading 144 games, doubleheaders in weeks 1, 2, 3 and 12, 40 of 48 possible division games clear of NFL byes and 9–9 home games, then the week-by-week matchup grid.

title: Both Halves of a Double-Header, Finally
summary: On a week where you play twice, Set Lineup now shows both games instead of one — and both leagues' lineup pages carry the matchup panel. Swipe between games on your phone, click the arrows on a laptop, and watch your projected total move on every card at once.
description: Double-headers are two opponents, two results, one lineup. TheLeague runs them in Weeks 1 through 3 and Week 13; the AFL has three of its own. Set Lineup never let on. It found the first game with your name on it, drew the matchup panel, and stopped — so half the week you were setting a lineup for simply wasn't on the page. If your second opponent was the one you needed to worry about, the page had nothing to say about them.

Now there's a card for each game. On a phone they sit side by side and snap under your thumb, with a dot for each and a small “Game 1 of 2” that keeps up as you swipe. On anything with a mouse, arrows sit on the panel and click through the same cards. A normal single-game week looks exactly as it always has — no dots, no arrows, nothing new to learn.

Each card knows its own game. Home and away follow the schedule, so you're on the right side of each scoreboard, and the projected total facing you is that opponent's, not a number borrowed from the other game. The one number both cards share is yours: MFL takes one lineup for the week and scores it twice, so every swap you make ticks your total on both cards at once. Watching one go up while the other sat there stale would have been its own kind of lie.

AFL owners get the whole thing at once. That page had no matchup panel at all — you set nine slots with no idea who they were pointed at. Now the same strip sits above the slots, each side wearing its franchise's colors and crest, with the projected score under it and a player of the game from each roster. Two opponents means two of those faceoffs, which is what a double-header week actually looks like.
imageAlt: The Set Lineup page for Week 1 showing a matchup card between Maverick and Pacific Pigskins with a player from each side, projected totals of 82.2 and 93.2, click arrows on the left and right of the panel, and a “Game 1 of 2” label with two dots below it.

title: Your Board Follows You to the Lineup Sheet
summary: Every starter and every bench player now carries your rank, right on the lineup screen — and when you open a slot, each eligible replacement does too. Free Agents and Rosters carry the board as well, and you can re-weight it without leaving the page.
description: Six sources loaded, weights tuned, a composite My Rank sitting there looking sharp — and then you opened the page where you actually pick someone, and none of it was there. That was most of a feature missing.

Set Lineup changes the most, and it's the one built for a phone. Every starter and every bench player now wears a small rank chip next to their projection, so the whole screen is scannable in one pass — the point being to notice the #41 sitting on your bench under the #75 you're starting. Open a slot and the sheet of eligible replacements carries a rank next to each name, with your current starter's rank on the card above it. That little “by Projection” line at the top of the list is a switch: tap it and the candidates reorder by your board, tap it again and they go back. Unranked players stay at the bottom either way, so nobody's kicker jumps the queue.

Over in the AFL, Free Agents and Rosters finally caught up to what The League has had for a while. Free Agents gets a View switch above the table — Stats keeps the columns you know, Rankings swaps in your board: My Rank first, then the sources actually feeding it. Not every source you've ever loaded, just the ones you ticked, capped at five, because a source you left out is one you've already said shouldn't weigh on the call. The table opens sorted by My Rank, best first, because that's the order you were going to put it in anyway, and every column sorts. Rosters gets one column next to each player, labeled with whose opinion it is: My Rank when you've built a composite, otherwise whatever board sits at the top of your list.

And you can argue with the board while you're looking at it. There's a My Rank button next to Filters on Free Agents and Rosters now that opens the sources and their weights right there — tick one in, push another down to 10%, watch the columns re-sort underneath you. Untick a source and its column leaves with it. The percentages still always total 100, so what you type is what that source is actually worth. Adding new imports and hiding built-ins still lives on Import Rankings; this is just the dial.

If you haven't loaded a board, none of this appears — no empty column, no dead button, no chips on your lineup. And the boards stay where you built them: your read on a player in one league is still a completely separate opinion from your read on him in the other.
imageAlt: The AFL Free Agents table in Rankings view with the My Rank editor open over it — a modal listing six ranking sources, three of them ticked with editable percentage weights, above a table showing only My Rank and the three sources feeding it: MFL ADP, ESPN and FantasySharks.

title: Your Draft Board, Already Built
summary: Import Rankings now arrives with six ranking sources already loaded and weighted — no bookmarklets, no setup, nothing to click. Tune the mix to taste with a weight you set as a percentage, and every league keeps a board of its own.
description: Open Import Rankings and there is already a board waiting. Six sources come loaded: MFL's own ADP from hundreds of real drafts, FantasySharks expert ranks, FantasyCalc dynasty trade values, Sleeper, ESPN redraft and ESPN superflex. Nothing to install, nothing to drag to a bookmarks bar, and it works on your phone. They refresh themselves every morning.

Which ones start switched on depends on the league, because the right opening board is not the same everywhere. The AFL and Best Ball lead with redraft ADP — you are re-drafting most of the roster, so a dynasty trade value overrates a 22-year-old you will not keep. TheLeague leads with dynasty values, because you are signing players to contracts. Every source is available in every league either way; only the starting three differ.

The mix is yours. Each source has a weight you set as a percentage — put ESPN superflex at 5 if you just want it whispering in the background, push MFL ADP to 60 if that is the board you actually trust. The numbers always total 100, so what you type is genuinely what that source is worth. Don't want the defaults at all? Hide them and build the whole thing from your own imports — the bookmarklets for FantasyPros, FootballGuys, DLF, KeepTradeCut, Yahoo and CBS are all still there.

One thing worth knowing if you play in more than one: every league now keeps its own board. What you build in the AFL stays in the AFL, TheLeague keeps exactly what you had, and Best Ball starts fresh instead of borrowing. Your own imports are untouched — the new sources simply sit alongside them.
imageAlt: The Import Rankings page with a Saved Rankings table listing six built-in sources — MFL ADP, FantasySharks, FantasyCalc, Sleeper, ESPN and ESPN Superflex — each with a My Rank checkbox, an editable percentage weight, a player count and View and Hide buttons, above the Get Bookmarklets grid.

title: Your Player, Your Position: The RotoWire Rule Now Says What It Meant
summary: RotoWire has always been the league's official depth chart, but the rulebook never spelled out who got to pick when RotoWire and MFL disagreed. You do — and you can flip him back and forth all season long.
description: Every year the same argument shows up in the group chat: RotoWire has your guy at tight end, MFL has him at wide receiver, and nobody can point to the line in the constitution that settles it. The line existed — "the commissioner will adjust the position as desired by the owner" — it just buried the important half of the sentence at the end.

So it now leads with it. When RotoWire and MFL list a player at different positions, the **owner** picks which of the two he carries. Not the commissioner, not whichever source loaded first. You ask, and the change lands before the upcoming week's kickoff.

The bigger clarification is the part that was never written down at all: that choice is not a one-time, season-long lock. A player the two sources disagree about is eligible at **both** positions for the entire season, and you can move him back and forth between them as often as you want. Ride him at tight end while the premium is worth it, slide him to receiver when your lineup math changes, slide him back in November. Each switch goes through the commissioner and takes effect before that week's kickoff, so the only real constraint is the deadline.

Two fences, because someone was going to ask. The only positions available are the ones MFL and RotoWire actually list — there is no third option hiding out there. And if both sources already agree on a player's position, there is nothing to choose; that is his position.
Ask Roger knows all of it now, too. The rules chat has a card on the position-change rule, and the constitution he answers from carries the clarified language.

title: The Dead Tile on Your Team Card Finally Says Something
summary: "Keepers — of 7 protected" has been sitting blank on the AFL homepage since the day it shipped, because there was never a number to put there. It's gone. In its place: your earned round-1 draft slot until the conference drafts wrap, then your last trophy for the rest of the year. The roster count next to it is finally counting this year's team, too.
description: If you have looked at your team card on the AFL homepage any time in the last while, you have seen a small grey dash where a keeper count was supposed to be. It was never going to be anything else. AFL does not have keepers the way MFL means keepers — the offseason auction wipes the slate every year — so the tile was measuring a thing that does not exist. Even if we had wired it up to the roster feed it would have read "7 of 7" for all twenty-four of you, which is a fact about the rules, not about your team.
So the slot now rotates with the calendar, and it always has something to say.

From June 1 until your conference finishes drafting, it shows your base draft position — the pick you earned out of last season's standings, run through the same tiebreaker chain the Draft Predictor uses. Smokane sits at 1.10 in the AL. If a trade has moved you off that slot, the number gets an asterisk and the line underneath tells you where you actually pick, so you can see both the pick you earned and the pick you own without opening another page.

Once the drafts are in the books it flips to hardware: the most recent title you have won, with your best one appended when the two are not the same trophy. That distinction turned out to matter for half the league. Smokane's most recent title is the 2025 AL North, which is real, and also not the thing worth leading with — so the tile reads AL North, then AFL '13. Ranking runs AFL Championship, Premier League, conference, division, D-League, NIT.

Four franchises have no hardware at all. Rather than hand them a counter of how long it has been, the tile falls through to the all-time record — the Micks have gone 78-72 since 2005, which reads a lot better than the alternative. And while we were in there: the roster count on that same card was reading off the season clock instead of the league clock, which meant it spent every offseason counting a team that no longer exists. It counts the roster you have right now — which, eight days out from the draft, is your seven keepers and nobody else.
imageAlt: The AFL homepage My Team card for Smokane FC with four tiles: Tier showing the Premier League badge, Conference showing the American League badge and North, Draft Slot showing 1.10 with AL · 2026 underneath, and Roster showing 7 with players underneath.

title: Your Bench Is on the Board Now
summary: Open any matchup on Live Scoring and there's a Bench drawer under your nine starters — every guy you left out, his real points, his real game clock. Collapsed by default, because some Sundays you don't want to know.
description: Live Scoring has only ever shown you the nine players who count. Which is the right nine to lead with, and also about half the story: the other question every owner is asking by 1:30 on a Sunday is whether the guy on his bench is having the day his starter isn't. Until now the only way to find out was to open MFL in another tab and read a table.

Tap into any matchup and there's a Bench section under the lineup. It opens onto both teams' benches side by side, grouped by position and sorted so the highest scorer at each spot is the first one you see — because the question is almost never "how did my bench do", it's "should I have started the other running back", and that answer needs the two of them near each other.

Every bench row is the full row: headshot, NFL team, the real game clock off the live scoreboard, the red-zone flag, the box-score line underneath. Same treatment as a starter, because a bench player having a huge afternoon is exactly as interesting as a starter having one — just considerably more painful.

It's collapsed by default and it's staying that way. The starters are the matchup and they get the top of the page; the bench is a second-guess and it can wait for you to ask. The summary bar shows each side's bench total, so you can decide from one glance whether you actually want to open it.

One thing the numbers deliberately don't do: count. Bench points never touch a team's score, its projected final or its win-probability bar — the drawer says so right at the top, and the feed keeps the two lists apart end to end so a bench touchdown can't wander into the scoring ticker either. Your 71.8 points of bench are a story, not a total.
imageAlt: The Live Scoring matchup detail with the Bench section expanded below the starting lineup. A summary bar reads 66.2 / 13 players on the left, BENCH in the middle, and 71.8 / 11 players on the right, with a note underneath saying bench points don't count toward the matchup. Below it, two columns headed Dangsters and Pigskins list each team's bench players grouped by position — quarterbacks first, then running backs and receivers — each with a position chip, headshot, NFL team logo, live points, projected final and game state.

title: The AFL Gets a Real Scoreboard
summary: All twenty-four franchises, both of your games, live on one page — with real NFL box-score lines under every starter, the actual game clock, red-zone alerts and a scoring-play ticker. No more refreshing MFL's message board on a Sunday.
description: Until today, watching your AFL week unfold meant a trip to MFL's live scoring summary — a page that tells you a number and nothing else. The league now has its own board at /afl-fantasy/live-scoring, and it is the same one TheLeague has been running, wired to AFL data end to end: your franchise's matchups pinned to the top, win-probability bars, projected finals, and a starter-by-starter breakdown when you tap in.

Because the AFL plays doubleheaders, the board shows all twenty-four matchups — every team's intra-conference game and its interconference game — and puts both of yours first. Tap either one and every starter carries his real NFL box-score line: "33/46, 394 yds, 2 TD · 14 car, 30 yds, 2 TD" under Josh Allen, "1 car, 3 yds · 7 rec (9 tgt), 76 yds" under Tyler Warren. The quarter and clock come off the live NFL scoreboard, not off a calculation, and a RED ZONE flag lights up next to any starter whose team has the ball inside the twenty.

The scoring ticker was the interesting part to get right here. The AFL's two conferences roster duplicate players — in a typical week, 85 of 131 starters are owned by more than one franchise — so "whose touchdown was that" has more than one answer. Attribute it to a single owner and roughly four in ten scoring plays quietly vanish from somebody's board. Every owner of every credited player now gets the row, which is the only version of this that is actually true.

Two honest gaps, both deliberate. Team defenses show their points and no stat line, because the NFL box score is keyed to individual players and a defense is not one — a plausible invented number sitting next to your real score is worse than a blank. And in the offseason, when MFL switches the live feed off, the page replays the last completed AFL regular-season week with a Sample Data badge on it rather than showing you an empty board.
imageAlt: The AFL Live Scoring matchup detail: Fullybaked 120.5 vs Ninjas 120.6, marked Final. Each starter row shows a position chip, headshot, NFL team and points, with a real box-score line underneath — Josh Allen reading "33/46, 394 yds, 2 TD · 14 car, 30 yds, 2 TD" and Tyler Warren "1 car, 3 yds · 7 rec (9 tgt), 76 yds". Below the rows a Scoring Plays section lists real fourth-quarter touchdowns with their game clock, each tagged TD.

title: Live Scoring Finally Knows What Actually Happened
summary: Every starter on the matchup page now carries his real box-score line, the quarter and clock come straight off the NFL scoreboard instead of being guessed, and the scoring ticker lists actual plays — with a red-zone flag that lights up the moment your guy's team gets inside the 20.
description: Live Scoring has always been able to tell you that your running back had 14.3 points. What it could never tell you was how — fourteen carries and a short touchdown, or one long screen and nothing else. Same number, completely different feeling about the rest of the afternoon. Now the line is right there under his name: "7 car, 55 yds · 3 rec (4 tgt), 20 yds, 1 TD". Quarterbacks get completions, yards, touchdowns and picks; kickers get their field goals and extra points; every skill player gets targets, which is the number you actually wanted.

The clock is the part we owe you an apology for. Until today the little "Q3 7:24" next to each player was not the game clock — it was arithmetic, MFL's remaining-game-seconds divided into quarters, and it drifted from the real one all afternoon because an NFL clock stops and that number does not. It now reads the actual scoreboard: "8:12 - 3rd", straight from ESPN. And when there is no game to read, it says "In progress" and no numbers at all, because a missing clock is a lot less annoying than a confident wrong one.

The scoring ticker used to guess too. It watched each starter's points between two one-minute polls, and if the number jumped it announced a scoring update at a made-up time — which meant a stat correction could invent a touchdown that never happened. It now lists real plays: "Q4 5:02 — Quentin Johnston 23 Yd pass from Justin Herbert (Cameron Dicker Kick)", in true chronological order across the whole slate, and only for plays your starters were actually part of.

New this week and best on a Sunday: a RED ZONE flag on any starter whose team has the ball inside the twenty, with the down and distance beside it. It is careful about whose red zone it is — your receiver does not get flagged because the other team is about to score on his defense, which is exactly the kind of thing that would have shipped if nobody checked.

Team defenses are the one gap, and it is on purpose. ESPN's box score is keyed to individual athletes and a defense is not one, so a DEF row shows its points and nothing else rather than a made-up stat line that disagrees with the score sitting next to it. Same rule everywhere else on the page: when the NFL feed is unreachable it tells you so out loud, instead of quietly showing you an empty board that looks like nobody did anything.
imageAlt: The Live Scoring matchup detail for Geeks 106.1 vs The Dream 106.8. Each starter row shows his position chip, headshot, NFL team, game state and points, with a real box-score line underneath — Justin Herbert reading "25/34, 318 yds, 3 TD · 7 car, 32 yds" and Derrick Henry "18 car, 169 yds, 2 TD · 1 rec (1 tgt), 13 yds · 1 FUM lost". Below the rows a Scoring Plays section lists real touchdowns with their quarter and game clock, each tagged TD.

title: Every Player Card Now Reads You In
summary: Tap a player anywhere on the site and the modal now opens with his latest ESPN headlines sitting right under the numbers — why the usage spiked, what camp is saying, whether the beat writers think the job is his. No more bouncing to another tab to find out what the box score was hinting at.
description: The player modal has always been good at telling you what happened. Sixty-two points, 5.2 a game, twelve starts — fine. What it could never tell you was why, and that is usually the part you actually opened it for. So you left, searched his name somewhere else, and came back.

Now the modal answers the question itself. Open any player and a Latest News block sits directly beneath his metrics, carrying his three most recent ESPN stories with a timestamp on each. Ryan Flournoy's card, for instance, currently leads with "Could Ryan Flournoy give Cowboys a third 1,000-yard receiver?" — which is a considerably more useful thing to know in August than his 2025 per-game average.

It is genuinely his news, not his team's. That distinction sounds pedantic and is the entire feature: a team-level feed hands every Falcon on your roster the same four headlines, and we measured it — the old approach returned 87 articles across 29 teams but only 28 different ones, with a Madden ratings piece filed under 27 of them. Pulling each player individually gets you 88% unique headlines instead of 32%.

Team defenses have no news feed of their own, so they borrow their best defender's and say so plainly rather than pretending the headlines belong to the unit. And when ESPN has nothing, the modal says it has nothing — it does not quietly show you stale filler, and if the feed itself is unreachable it tells you that instead, with a retry, because "no news" and "we couldn't reach the wire" are very different things to tell an owner.
imageAlt: The player detail modal for Ryan Flournoy: the team-colored hero band with his name, position and draft details, a three-card metrics strip showing 62.6 points and 5.2 per game, then a Latest News section listing three recent ESPN stories with type labels and timestamps, above the Season Results table.

title: The Pecking Order Explains Itself
summary: The column doesn't publish again until the Tuesday after Week 1, so its page spent the preseason showing last season's rankings with nothing to say they were last season's. It now opens with what the column actually is — the formula, the awards, the date the first real issue lands — and stamps the issue underneath it as a sample.
description: The Pecking Order arrived three days ago and immediately went quiet for a month, because there is nothing to rank until Week 1 has been played. That left both leagues with a page that opened cold on a set of rankings from last December: real numbers, real teams, a live-looking headline, and no way for anyone who had never heard of the column to tell that none of it was current.

The page now knows which of those two situations it is in. Out of season it leads with the column itself — every Tuesday morning, every team in your league ranked top to bottom, and a plain-English pass at the math. Half your score is your all-play record, which runs your points against every other team in the league instead of the one you happened to draw: post the fourth-best score in a given week and the week is worth beating everybody but three, whether you won by 40 or lost by 2. The other half is your last three weeks, so a hot month moves you and one bad Sunday in Week 2 stops following you around in November.

Under that, the six things every issue carries — the ranking cards with their movement arrows, Stat of the Week, Bench Blunder, Heater, Cooler, next week's Matchup of the Week, and the full standings and all-play tables. And the date, spelled out: the first real issue of the season lands Tuesday, September 15, the Tuesday after Week 1.

The issue below all that is still there, still real, and now clearly labelled a sample — a past week published so you can see the format, with its publish date dropped so nothing about it reads as breaking news. The moment a real issue exists for the season being played, every bit of the explainer disappears and the page goes back to leading with this week's verdict.
Both leagues get it from the same component, so neither drifts, and it re-arms itself every February when the season ends.
imageAlt: The AFL Pecking Order landing page in its preseason state: a 'New weekly column' eyebrow above the title, a lede explaining the Tuesday-morning column, the date of the first issue, and six cards covering the formula, the awards and the standings snapshot.

title: Weekly Fixes & Polish (Aug 10-18)
summary: 26 bug fixes and style improvements across rosters, other, rankings, schefter report, and more.
description: This week's 26 bug fixes and polish improvements touched the following areas of the site:

Rosters — The Analytics tab was shoving the whole roster page off the side of your screen. On a laptop, a small window, or a tablet held sideways, the team card at the top ran right past the edge — the team drawer would open and half the league's crests were somewhere out in the dark to the right, with the East and Southwest divisions simply gone. The card was innocent. Down at the bottom of the Analytics tab there's a Players by Team report that lays its cards out three across, and three of those cards need about a thousand pixels between them — more than the screen had. Rather than stack, they insisted, and everything above them stretched to match. They now count the room first and take two across, or one, depending on what's actually available. Three-across is still what you get on a wide monitor, which is the only place it ever fit. The bottom of the roster page's team card was a pileup. Three things were trying to occupy the same strip of air: the little word under the view tabs telling you which one you're on, the arrow that opens the team drawer, and the edge of the card itself. Retired names and standings abbreviations now go through untouched when they're plainly being used as words — lowercase, in the middle of a sentence. Roger's links in the group chat work again. When he ended a sentence with a link — "Review your plan at theleague.us/rosters." — GroupMe grabbed the period along with the address and sent everyone who tapped it to a page that doesn't exist. Two fixes, because one wasn't enough: every bot message now gets the trailing period trimmed off the link on the way out, and the site itself now catches a link that arrives with a period stuck to it and quietly sends you to the right page instead of a dead end. Music City Mafia's dark-mode crest is real artwork now. The new one puts the man, the hat and the skyline on their own near-black backdrop with the outline drawn in properly. Same guy, same cigar, no longer looking like a sticker somebody cut out. The Mariachi Ninjas get a proper dark-mode crest, and both leagues share it. The old dark file was the ordinary crest with a white line around it and is gone. Both leagues wear the identical new one, so the Ninjas finally look the same on either side after dark. The page now reads the draft results: before and during the rookie draft the class stays tucked away like always, and once the final pick is in the books, the leftovers show up by default. Clearing filters respects whichever default the calendar says. Ashton Dulin went to Malone University, a school so small ESPN doesn't keep a logo for it — and instead of shrugging, the Free Agents table rendered a broken-image icon and the school's full name, inflating his row to twice the height of everyone else's. Small-school players now get a tidy dash in the college column (the name's still there on hover). Bonus find while we were in there: the Ragin' Cajuns' logo had been pointing at Louisiana Christian University — a school with no logo either — since forever, so Louisiana products like Elijah Mitchell finally wear the actual fleur-de-lis.

Navigation & Routing — Search on TheLeague's site was pulling AFL-only pages into its results — type "keeper" looking for a rules question and you'd land on the AFL's Keeper Planner instead, a page that doesn't even apply to TheLeague's roster rules. The site directory is shared infrastructure across both leagues; TheLeague's search now only shows TheLeague's own pages.

That's corrected, so the crests sit at their proper weight across the site. One knock-on: the countdown banners use the dark badge on their navy panel no matter which mode you're in, so their crest is a touch larger now in daylight too. The playoff standings card on the AFL homepage stopped labeling its division leaders with the word "Div". The top two seeds in your conference are there because they won their division, and the card marked that with a tiny grey pill reading DIV — accurate, and telling you nothing you couldn't already work out from the two rows sitting at the top. It's now the actual division shield: the same AL North, AL South, NL East and NL West artwork hanging on those teams' trophy walls, shrunk down to ride beside the crest. The win-year stamp is scrubbed off it, because this one isn't a trophy — it's a standing, and it can change on Sunday. Both leagues' badges were already drawn to read on a white card and a navy one alike, so nothing had to be redrawn for dark mode.

Playoffs — And then there was one. 2004 was the last season we couldn't rebuild — six divisions feeding an eight-team bracket meant the playoff field wasn't simply the top four in each conference, and without knowing who actually qualified there were three different ways to read that season's games. The fix came from an unexpected direction: the NIT. Sixteen teams played in it, the league has twenty-four, and nobody plays in both — so identifying the NIT field identified the championship field by subtraction. The AFL Losers Bracket then accounted for six of those eight, leaving exactly two teams standing, and MFL's own records name the winner: Bukkake Warriors 133.6, Your Team Sucks 106.44. Every game of 2004 is now on the page, from that title game down to the wonderfully named "2nd and 3rd Round NIT Losers." That's twenty seasons rebuilt. The only one left blank is 2003, which was played on Yahoo and never existed in MFL at all. 2011 finally has a playoff bracket, and it took some doing. Every other season we rebuilt by assuming the playoff field was the top four in each conference — which is how the AFL seeds it, except in 2011, when six divisions fed an eight-team bracket and two teams from outside the top eight got in on division titles. Feed the wrong eight teams into a bracket and it falls apart immediately, which is exactly what happened. So instead of guessing the qualification rule, the site now works backward from the shape: find the four week-14 games whose winners play each other in week 15, whose winners meet in week 16. Only one arrangement of that season's games fits, and it turned out to be Delirium Tremens over Drunk Indians 154.94 to 147.95. All ten of 2011's brackets are now on the page, from the title game down to NIT Consolation 2L, and every one was checked against the league's own bracket pages. 2003 stays blank forever — that was the Yahoo year, and MFL never had the games. Eighteen years of AFL playoffs came back from the dead. Pick any season before 2024 and the brackets page said "Bracket data not available" — for the championship, for the NIT, for all of it. Turns out the games were never missing. MFL's bracket export only ever handed us seed numbers for those years, but the schedule had every playoff week sitting right there, fully scored, the whole time. The page now walks those weeks back into a bracket, so 2005 through 2023 finally show real matchups with real teams and real point totals: Cougs over Smokane, Chatmaster over the Limp Ditkas, No Frills over More Cowbell. One season stays blank: 2003, the year the league played on Yahoo, so MFL never had the games at all. The consolation brackets are back too, which is the half of the postseason that actually decided things. The AFL Losers Bracket, the 3rd and 5th and 7th place games, and that magnificent tower of NIT losers brackets that handed out draft picks — all of it was blank for every season before 2024, and all of it is now filled in from the schedule. Worth knowing while you browse: MFL's own results page lies about finishing order for these years. The league wrote custom titles into its brackets, MFL read those titles as placements, and so it lists Da Dangsters second in 2005 when they actually finished third — they won the Losers Bracket. Second place was Smokane, who lost the title game to the Cougs. The brackets now on the page are built from games, not titles, so they show what actually happened. The NIT tab was empty for fifteen seasons, and the reason is deeply stupid. The page decided which brackets were the championship and which were the NIT by their ID number — brackets 1 through 5 were the big dance, 6 through 9 were the NIT. That's true from 2018 on. It is not true for 2005 (NIT is bracket 3), or 2006 (bracket 4), or anything from 2007 to 2017 (bracket 5). So for fifteen years the NIT was quietly filed under Championship while the NIT tab sat there with nothing in it. The page now goes by the bracket's actual name, which has said "NIT" on it since 2003. The NIT Champion payout shows up for those seasons too, and the AFL Cup — an in-season thing from the 2012-2016 era that MFL never exported a single game for — stopped padding the page with seven empty cards. The AFL playoff bracket was seeding old seasons with today's map. Pull up 2005 and the page sorted everyone into the four divisions the league runs now — except 2005 had six, three per conference, with a Central and a Pacific that haven't existed in over a decade. Twelve conference races between 2003 and 2016 came out seeded differently on the playoffs page than on the standings page for that very same season, which is a neat trick for a site to pull on itself. The playoffs page now reads each season's real structure, the same way standings already did. The AFL had been quietly wearing TheLeague's green. The word "Championship" over each playoff bracket was green. The OFFICIAL badge on the draft order page was a green pill. The checkmark next to the AFL in the league switcher — on every page — was green. So were the read-more links on What's New, the tier badge in the asset library, Roger's reply rail on the homepage feed, and the accent on the homepage's What's New banner. None of it was a mistake anyone would file a report about; it's just that green belongs to the other league, and the two sites share enough plumbing that a color wanders across the border without anyone noticing. Most of these weren't even on AFL pages — they live in parts shared by both leagues that nobody had ever taught to tell the leagues apart. The bracket labels now read in the trophy gold the championship badges already use, and everything else is AFL red. The gold had to be picked twice, once per mode: the amber that reads on a white card turns to mud on a navy one, so at night it switches to the metallic gold off the award art. TheLeague looks exactly as it did. The AFL playoffs page had a shadow inside a shadow. Every bracket on it — the championship, the AL and NL semis, the third-place game, the whole tower of placement games below them — sits inside one big card, and each one was also casting its own drop shadow onto that card. That would be fine if a bracket were a card, but it isn't: it's a stack of matchups with no surface and no rounded corners of its own, so the shadow had nothing to hug and drew a hard rectangle around each bracket instead. In daylight it was faint enough to pass for a deliberate divider. At night it was a row of dark boxes ruled across a dark card, square corners and all, sitting inside the card's own shadow — which is where the doubled-up look came from. The brackets now let the card do the lifting, which is what the card is for. TheLeague's playoffs page never had this and didn't need touching, so the two finally match again.

Standings — Settled a tiebreaker argument nobody knew we were having. Both rulebooks list 'Most Points Allowed' near the bottom of the standings tiebreakers — the idea being that if you're dead even with someone and you had to survive a tougher schedule of beatings, that should work in your favor. The code read it backwards and quietly rewarded the team that gave up FEWER points. Now a team that allowed more points wins that step, which means both the better spot in the standings and the earlier draft pick. Fair warning: this has never actually decided anything. In 76 seasons of TheLeague divisions and 106 of the AFL's, no tie has ever made it that far down the list. It's fixed for the day one finally does.

Rosters — Managing a player in dark mode was a flashbang. Tap the three dots next to anyone on your AFL roster and the action menu came up as a stark white card — and worse, the player's name came up white ON that white card, so the one thing you needed to read was the one thing you couldn't. The card, the four action rows, the confirmation copy and the success and error banners now all wear the same navy the rest of the site does, with the AFL red showing up on hover where it belongs. Light mode looks exactly like it did yesterday.

Navigation & Routing — In dark mode, the Premier League link in the sidebar menu was a crest you couldn't see. The badge is navy, the dark menu is navy, and the two met in the middle — leaving a label with a smudge where its logo should be. The rest of the site has had a dark version of that crest for a while, ringed with a halo so it reads against a dark background; the menu was the one place still loading the light-mode file off an old external address. It now uses the same artwork everything else does, D-League included, and it's served from our own site rather than fetched from elsewhere. Light mode is unchanged, except the crest no longer gets squashed into a square.

Free Agents — Ashton Dulin went to Malone University, a school so small ESPN doesn't keep a logo for it — and instead of shrugging, the Free Agents table rendered a broken-image icon and the school's full name, inflating his row to twice the height of everyone else's. Small-school players now get a tidy dash in the college column (the name's still there on hover). Bonus find while we were in there: the Ragin' Cajuns' logo had been pointing at Louisiana Christian University — a school with no logo either — since forever, so Louisiana products like Elijah Mitchell finally wear the actual fleur-de-lis.

description: This week's 11 bug fixes and polish improvements touched the following areas of the site:

Other — Both sites got lighter on their feet. Every page request was quietly hauling around twenty years of archived league feeds — every roster, every box score, every player list back to 2004 — loaded fresh whether you were looking at last Sunday or the Bush administration. It was 165 megabytes of luggage, and the worst part is we were carrying two copies of it: the pages that show old seasons already have their own, so the second set was along for the ride and nothing more. The site had grown so heavy it had actually stopped being able to deploy. Now only the last three seasons ride along and the archives are pulled up when something actually asks for them, which cut the whole thing roughly in half. Nothing you can see has changed — every season is still there, still complete — it just gets there faster. Schefter stopped chewing holes in his own tips. To keep him from naming a team he's not allowed to name, every tip gets scrubbed before he reads it — any franchise name in the text is swapped out for "[a team]." Trouble is, the list of names he watches for includes short ones that are also just... words. "Dead Cap Walking" goes by DEAD in the standings and spent six seasons as Heavy Chevy, so a tip reading "deal is dead, but he's a heavy favorite to be cut" reached him as "deal is [a team], but he's a [a team] favorite." That second half matters, because the messages already sitting in the chat can't be edited — and it works for links you paste into a text message or an email too. The Mariachi Ninjas get a proper dark-mode crest, and both leagues share it. The site can trace a thin ring around a dark logo to keep it readable at night, which is a fine safety net and never as good as artwork drawn for the job — so the green ring got drawn into the logo itself instead of being painted on at the last second by a stylesheet. The old dark file was the ordinary crest with a white line around it and is gone. Both leagues wear the identical new one, so the Ninjas finally look the same on either side after dark. Your phone was occasionally serving you a page from a previous visit and passing it off as live. The site keeps an offline copy of pages so there's something to show when you're in a dead zone — but it was reaching for that copy any time a request didn't complete cleanly, including the extremely normal case of tapping a second link before the first one finished loading. The saved copy could be days old and still point at a stylesheet that no longer exists, which is how a page could come up looking half-built and then quietly right itself a few taps later. It's back in the heading now, starting on the same left edge as everything else and reading like a byline. It also shows up on phones, which it never did before: the old version hid itself on anything under 1300 pixels wide, because below that there was no margin left to hide in.

title: The 2017 Trophy Nobody Was Holding: the AFL Cup Comes Back, and Smokane FC Gets It
summary: 2017's all-play season was the last AFL Cup — not the "Founders Table" we made up for it — and it ended in week 16, not 17. That one week moves the title to Smokane FC.
description: Two things were wrong about 2017, and the second one only became visible once the first was fixed.

Start with the name. That season ran as one 24-team all-play table, the format the Premier League and D-League grew out of the year after, and we shipped it under a heading called the "Founders Table." Nobody in the league has ever called it that. We invented it. The league called it what it had called the same competition for the two seasons before: the AFL Cup. The Cup did not die in 2016 — it changed shape, traded a knockout bracket for a table, and ran one more year before the split replaced it. It says AFL Cup on the standings page now, and the trophy room treats 2017 as the Cup's last season instead of pretending it never happened.

Then the week. Every one of these tables gets cut off somewhere, the site was using week 17 for all of them, and 2017 ended at week 16. One week does not sound like much. It is the entire competition here. Through week 16 Smokane FC finishes 259-109 and Fullybaked 258-110 — one all-play win apart, out of 368. Play the extra week and Fullybaked passes them. The site had been showing the week-17 answer under a name the league never used, so the 2017 AFL Cup had effectively been awarded to the wrong team and filed under the wrong competition. What settled it was not the math: the commissioner went and checked what the league actually paid out that season, and the Cup money went to Smokane FC.

Smokane FC's trophy room gains an AFL Cup badge stamped 2017, its eighteenth piece of hardware. Nothing else about that season moves: Thundering Herd keeps the 2017 AFL Championship they won in that week-16 final, and the promotion line is untouched — the top 12 is the same twelve franchises whichever week you stop at, and it still matches the 2018 Premier League roster exactly. The cutoff week is now recorded per season rather than assumed, so no future era can quietly inherit the wrong finish line.

title: Twenty-Two Seasons of Extremes, Finally Countable
summary: The AFL Record Book is live — highest scores, biggest blowouts, closest finishes, longest streaks and the most-played rivalries, drawn from all 5,333 games the league has ever played.
description: Here is a thing that was quietly impossible until this week: naming the biggest blowout in AFL history. MFL's archives had handed back 2007 through 2019 with the regular-season matchups stripped out, so any all-time list you built stopped being about the league and started being about whichever years happened to survive. Those seasons have now been pulled back in and checked against the official standings, and the Record Book is what you do with them.

It answers the questions that come up in the chat every year. The biggest blowout ever is Your Team Sucks over Joey's Team by 136.16 — in 2004, a season that was almost entirely invisible on this site until now. The closest finish is one hundredth of a point: The Mariachi Ninjas 110.77, The Boondock Saints 110.76, week 9 of 2015. The highest single game belongs to Drunk Indians, 231.72 in 2021. The longest winning streak is 16 straight by Whitman's Wonders, running from week 11 of 2011 into week 4 of 2012, and the longest losing streak is 16 as well, by Badd Boys, which took them from week 5 of 2015 to week 2 of 2016.

There are ten boards in total: highest single game, biggest blowout, closest finish, highest combined score, longest winning and losing streaks, most-played and most lopsided rivalries, best regular season and most points in a season. Every rivalry and every game links straight through to the pairing page, so you can go from "we got destroyed once" to the full series in one tap.

Two deliberate choices worth knowing about. Franchises appear under the name they carried that season — Cliffside Killer Clowns, Dicks out for Harambe, Taco Hell — because a record book that renames history is a worse record book. And forfeits are excluded: a 0.00 is not a performance, and letting them in would have handed "biggest blowout" to games nobody played.

One permanent hole, printed on the page rather than hidden: the AFL played its 2003 season on Yahoo and only the standings were ever typed into MFL. No game from that year has a score anywhere, so nothing from it can appear. Every season from 2004 on is complete.
imageAlt: The AFL Record Book page: ten leaderboard cards across three columns — highest single game, biggest blowout, closest finish, highest combined score, longest winning and losing streaks, most-played and most lopsided rivalries, best regular season and most points in a season — each listing five ranked records with team names, scores and the season they happened.

title: The Pecking Order Comes to the AFL
summary: Claude Schefter's Tuesday-morning column now runs in the AFL too — all 24 franchises ranked 1 through 24, with trend arrows, five weekly awards, and a conference-by-conference standings snapshot. Half your all-play record, half your last three weeks, and not one ounce of credit for the schedule doing you a favor.
description: TheLeague has spent a season being told, every Tuesday morning, exactly where it stands. The AFL has spent that same season with 24 teams, two conferences, four divisions and no single page willing to say which of them is actually any good. That page exists now.

The math is the same argument it is on the other side of the site, and it is deliberately a short one. Half of your score is your all-play record — if you had played every team every week, how often would you have won? The other half is your last three weeks of scoring. Both halves are scaled against the field before they are added, so fifty-fifty means fifty-fifty. Your head-to-head record does not vote. That is the entire point: the column exists to look past the thing the standings already tell you.

In a 24-team league that distinction has teeth. Look at the Week 14 issue and Balls Deep sit second on a .638 all-play while riding a four-game losing streak, and Vitside Mafia jumped three spots on a 3-1 stretch that the standings barely register. Both of those are the formula arguing with the record, out loud, in public.

Underneath the rankings: Stat of the Week, Bench Blunder of the Week (the AFL leaves a genuinely upsetting number of points on the bench), Heater, Cooler, and next week's Matchup of the Week, picked as the highest-ranked clash on the slate. Then a standings snapshot split the way the AFL actually thinks — American League North and South, National League East and West — with the full 24-team all-play table beside it.

One AFL-specific wrinkle worth knowing: the league plays double-header weeks, and the column counts them honestly. The record beside each team covers the last three weeks it played, not the last three games, so a doubleheader shows up as "3-1 over their last 4" instead of quietly dropping a game on the floor.

Two issues are up now — 2025 Weeks 13 and 14 — so you can see the trend arrows working. From kickoff, a fresh one lands every Tuesday morning, and Schefter announces it in the chat with the top of the order and the week's worst bench decision.
imageAlt: The AFL Pecking Order Week 14 issue: Schefter's headline and lede above the 1-24 rankings, each card showing the team crest, a one-line verdict, and its all-play percentage, last-three-week PPG, season PPG and composite score.

title: The Pecking Order Stops Grading on Five Curves
summary: Two things decide the rankings now: your all-play record and your last three weeks. Fifty-fifty, and the team colors are finally readable in dark mode.
description: The Pecking Order used to blend five ingredients — recent form, head-to-head record, all-play percentage, season PPG and average margin — which sounds thorough and mostly meant nothing moved. Two of those five measure the same thing twice (season PPG and margin are both "you score a lot"), and head-to-head record is the one number the whole column exists to look past. Win a shootout by half a point and lose a 130-point week to the league leader, and the old formula quietly rewarded you for both.

It is now half your all-play record and half your last three weeks. All-play asks the only fair season-long question there is: if you played everybody every week, how often would you win? The rolling three-week scoring average asks the other one: are you any good right now? Nothing else votes. Season PPG and average margin still show on every card as context — they just do not move you anymore.

Both halves are scaled against the field before they are added, so fifty-fifty means fifty-fifty. On an absolute scale a league full of all-play numbers bunched between .300 and .700 would have quietly counted for about half as much as the scoring side, which is exactly the kind of thing that hides in a five-ingredient blend.

The visible effect: teams whose record is better than their football stop coasting, and teams getting beaten by the schedule stop being buried. In this week's issue Da Dangsters climb to #3 on a .710 all-play, and Wascawy Wabbits — a .659 all-play team scoring 93 a week lately — sit at #8, which is exactly the argument the two halves are supposed to have.

Separately, and long overdue: every team accent on the page was being rendered in the franchise's raw brand color, which is fine until dark mode. Bring The Pain is near-black and Cowboy Up is navy, so their rank numbers were effectively invisible on a dark card; in light mode Midwestside's yellow had the same problem against white. Every franchise color on the site now resolves to a version that stays readable on whatever theme you're in, brand-accurate where it already worked, nudged only where it did not.
imageAlt: The Pecking Order Week 17 rankings in dark mode, each card showing a readable team-colored rank number alongside the team's all-play percentage, last-three-week PPG, season PPG and composite score.

title: Roger Can Be Wrong. Now You Can Say So Without Deleting the Question.
summary: Every Ask Roger card gets a “This answer looks wrong” button. Report it, say why, and the commissioner sees it — the question stays right where it is.
description: Two of Roger's answers turned out to be wrong this month, and both took an embarrassingly long time to catch. The taxi squad ruling stood for seventeen days. The 5th-year option card had the wrong salary formula on it since March. In both cases somebody read the wrong answer, moved on, and nobody had a way to say anything.

That's because there wasn't one. The only lever on a bad answer was the commissioner's delete button, and deleting is a blunt instrument — it throws away the question along with the answer. The owner who asked it loses their card, their name comes off it, and the next person with the same question starts from scratch. So nothing got deleted, and wrong answers just sat there.

Now every card has a “This answer looks wrong” button. Hit it, optionally type what's actually wrong, and it's logged. The card picks up a red banner so the next owner scrolling past knows not to lean on it, and the commissioner sees who reported it and why. Changed your mind? Undo it. Nothing gets deleted, ever.

Worth knowing: this works on the pinned League Office cards too, not just the ones Roger writes on the fly. The 5th-year option mistake was on a hand-written card, which is exactly the kind nobody thinks to double-check. And a correction to the rulebook still doesn't rewrite an answer that's already on the page — Roger writes each one once and it stays written — so flagging it is what actually gets it looked at.
imageAlt: An Ask Roger card about the 5th-year team option showing a red banner reading “2 owners reported this answer as wrong — the commissioner is reviewing it”, the list of reporting teams and their reasons, and a “You reported this — undo” button.

title: Twenty-Three Years of Grudges, Finally Written Down
summary: AFL franchise pages now carry an all-time record, single-game highlights, a top-five rivals list and a full trade ledger — plus a brand-new rivalry matrix showing what every franchise has done to every other one since 2004.
description: The AFL franchise page has spent its whole life showing you a trophy wall and a name history and then just… stopping. No record. No points. No sense of whether this franchise has been good for twenty years or good for one. That page now opens with the numbers: all-time record, win percentage, seasons played, career points, points per game, playoff appearances. Smokane FC, for the record, is 232-157 across 23 seasons with 46,022 points. That is a lot of football nobody could see until today.

Underneath it: Single-Game Highlights. Your best day ever, your worst day ever, and the two blowouts — the one you handed out and the one you took. Then Top Rivals, which is the part worth arguing about. It ranks opponents on how charged the series actually is, not just how often you played: an even record counts for more than a lopsided one, and playoff meetings count triple. Smokane's list is led by Fullybaked — 14-9 across 23 games with seven playoff meetings, which is more postseason history than most franchises have with anyone.

Every rival links to a full pairing page: the whole series in one table, every meeting since 2004, with closest game, biggest blowout, highest combined score and longest winning streak on top. Those pages know what round each playoff game was, too — Quarterfinal, Semifinal, AL and NL Conference Championships, NIT Championship, the whole ladder. And there is now a Rivalry Matrix under Franchises, split by conference, where you can read one franchise's record against all eleven of its conference-mates in a single row and see the hot pairings shaded red.

Last piece: the Trade Ledger. Every deal this franchise has ever made, grouped by year, with what went out, what came back, and the trade comment the owner typed at the time. Each partner links straight to your rivalry page with them, because a trade history and a grudge history are the same history.

One caveat when this shipped, since resolved: MFL's archived exports returned 2007-2019 with the regular-season matchups stripped, so head-to-head totals under-counted badly and leaned toward playoff games — Smokane's rivalry pages covered 233 of its 389 career games. Those seasons have since been recovered from MFL's authenticated schedule view and verified against the official standings, so every AFL season from 2004 on is now complete: Smokane's pages carry all 462 of its meetings. title: The Audit Comes for TheLeague: 8 Division Banners Change Hands, and 2022 Comes Back From the Dead
summary: Same homebrew tiebreaker, same bad math — this time in TheLeague's record books. MFL's official standings are now the source of truth, eight division titles just moved, and an entire missing season got its wins back.
description: Fresh off auditing the AFL's record books, we pointed the same flashlight at TheLeague. Same rot. The code crowning each division winner sorted by raw division record FIRST, which is not a thing the constitution says anywhere. Read the rulebook: division record is tiebreaker number two. Overall record wins the division. What that bug produced was ten seasons where a team with a worse record got the banner because it happened to beat up on its own division — 2020 Eastern went to a 12-6 club over a 14-4 one, and the 2025 Northwest and Southwest were both handed to the runner-up. Eight of those ten are banners you can actually see change hands on a franchise page; the other two (2015 Central, 2018 Southwest) went to teams from an earlier ownership era, so nobody's page was showing them either way.

So we did what we did for the AFL: stopped re-deriving history and went to the source. MFL applies the constitution's full tiebreaker chain itself, and its official standings order now decides every division title. If you want the single case that settles the argument, it's 2015 Central. Amish Rakefighters and The Executioners both finished 15-3, both went 4-2 in the division. The Executioners scored more points AND had the better all-play record, so every version of our math picked them. MFL picked Amish — because Amish swept the season series, 120.66-91.19 in Week 1 and 136.34-127.01 in Week 3. Head-to-head. Step one. It's the one tiebreaker our code could never see, because the standings feed doesn't carry it.

Then there was 2022, which the record books had simply lost. MFL's export for that season ships the win-loss columns in a different shape, and our reader was looking for the wrong one — so every franchise in TheLeague was carrying a 0-0-0 for 2022 while somehow having scored two thousand points. No division titles, no wins, no losses, a whole year of football filed under nothing. It's back: Vitside Mafia's 15-3, Dark Magicians' 14-4, all four division winners, and roughly a hundred and forty games returned to career records across the league.

We also went looking for the titles nobody could claim. Twenty-five division championships were won under a previous owner of a franchise slot — Amish Rakefighters, LBer-DeCleaters, Acer FC Edge, the Sabertooths — and because career stats follow the human and not the jersey, those banners had nowhere to live and were silently dropped from the record entirely. They're now written down under the names that won them, which is the necessary first step; putting them somewhere you can actually look at them is a job for another day. Meanwhile every standings page in TheLeague renders MFL's official order, and a regression suite locks all of it down so no homebrew math ever crawls back into the record books.

title: Justice Is Served: Thundering Herd Is Dead, Long Live "A Bruin Pegs Me"
summary: Two titles, three conference crowns, and a proud dynasty — none of it matters when you finish dead last in the D-League. Franchise 0014 has been served its punitive rename, and the record books already know it.
description: The D-League doesn't grade on a curve, and it definitely doesn't care about your trophy case. Franchise 0014 — two-time champion, three-time NL conference king, the Herd desk's own nostalgia machine — bottomed out the standings this season, and the league's oldest tradition came for its name. Thundering Herd is retired. "A Bruin Pegs Me" is what's stitched on the jersey now.

The old name isn't erased, just filed where it belongs: the franchise page's history tab still remembers every era back to 2003, the current owner keeps every year of stats and hardware they earned along the way, and the site's search bar will still find you if you type "Herd" out of muscle memory.

And the paperwork has now caught up. The new crest and banner are live across the site — a UCLA cheerleader in powder blue and gold, bat in hand, which for an owner who bleeds cardinal and gold is the part that actually stings. The franchise's brand colors moved to navy and gold to match, so every roster row, matchup card and player headshot backdrop wears it too. Thirteen trophies, third-most in the league, all still on the wall above it.

title: The Record Books Get an Audit: 22 Division Titles Restored to Their Rightful Owners
summary: Historical AFL division titles were being computed with a homebrew tiebreaker instead of the constitution. MFL's official standings are now the source of truth — and 22 banners just changed hands, from 2004 all the way to last season.
description: Somewhere along the way, the site's record books started freelancing. When we backfilled two decades of AFL history, the code crowning each division's champion sorted by division record first — and at one point even used raw points-for as a tiebreaker. That's not how this league works. The constitution is clear: overall record wins the division, and ties run the full gauntlet — head-to-head, division record, conference record, Power Rank, points, all-play, victory points, most points allowed, coin flip. MFL has been applying those exact rules all along.

So we stopped re-deriving history and went to the source. MFL's official final standings now decide every division title, every season, 2004 through 2025 — and an independent recomputation using the constitution's own tiebreaker chain agrees with MFL in all 100-plus division-seasons on the books. The fallout: 22 division banners moved to their rightful owners. Dicks out for Harambe's 12-5 season finally beats a 9-8 record for the 2025 AL South crown. Chatmaster's 14-3 masterpiece in 2017 takes the NL West it always deserved. And the all-time trophy count has a new king: the Drunk Indians, at 19 pieces of hardware, with Smokane FC sliding to second at 17.

The standings pages got the same treatment — historical and current standings now render in MFL's official order on every AFL surface, so the trophy room, the standings page, and the playoff picture finally tell the same story. A regression suite now locks all of this in so no homebrew math ever sneaks back into the record books.

title: The Keeper Report Card: Hindsight Is Undefeated
summary: A new Claude Schefter report grades every AFL keeper class by the only judge that matters — what actually happened. Your 2024 roster re-ranked by 2025 points, the seven you should have kept highlighted, and every hit, miss, and the-one-that-got-away called out by name. A keeper is worth the points he scored in the games you could have started him — backups count a fraction — so the grade is about the call you made, not the roster you inherited. Flip to 2026 to see this year's classes waiting for kickoff.
description: You had all offseason. You studied the roster, you agonized over the seventh spot, you declared your keepers with the quiet confidence of a person who has definitely not just protected a running back about to lose his job in training camp. And then the season happened. The Keeper Report Card is where those two stories meet: every franchise's previous-season roster, re-ranked by what those players scored the following year, with the hindsight-optimal seven highlighted in green.

Every keep gets a verdict. Keep a top-seven scorer? Hit. Keep someone who finished ninth on your own roster? Miss. Let a top-seven scorer walk back into the draft pool? That's the one that got away, and yes, it's labeled in yellow so everyone can see it. The league summary up top crowns the best keeper class, names the worst keeper decisions, and tallies the misses league-wide.

Here is the part that decides the table, and it's mercifully simple: a player is worth the points he scored in the games you could actually have started him. The optimal seven have to fit a real lineup — one QB, one kicker, one defense, and six from RB/WR/TE — because a third quarterback with nowhere to play isn't a keeper, he's a paperweight with a clipboard.

Every class is then scored on the share of its own ceiling it captured: the value your keepers delivered, divided by the value of the seven you could have kept. That grades the call instead of the collection — the ceiling swings roughly 2x from the league's thinnest roster to its deepest, and nobody chose the roster they inherited. Max out a thin roster and you'll beat a rival who left points on a loaded one.

Backups aren't written off — they're credited the share of their points they'd realistically have played. A seventh skill player rotates in across six flex starters' byes and matchups, so he counts 7/10 of his points. A second quarterback, kicker, or defense only plays the starter's bye week and the odd matchup call, so he counts 1/10. Both are “backups” and they are nowhere near equally valuable — bench keeps are marked Bench and priced accordingly.

Kickers and defenses aren't excluded from anything. Your starting kicker's points are real points at a real lineup slot, and passing on a big-leg season can be a genuine miss. A second kicker, though, counts a tenth of his points — which is the polite way of saying stop stockpiling kickers.

The bottom of the page spells out the whole rubric, because a report card that doesn't tell you how it grades is just a number with an attitude. The page defaults to the last finished season while we wait on kickoff. Once the 2026 games start, the grades go live and update all year — check back weekly to watch your genius (or your shame) accumulate in real time.
imageAlt: The Keeper Report Card: league summary tiles for the best keeper class and the worst keeper decisions, each scored as a share of optimal, above per-franchise rosters ranked by points with Kept, Miss, and Got Away badges.

The cards sort by hardware first, wins second, inside proper American League and National League sections, and each one glows in its team color when you reach for it. The icon stays — this is the AFL, we lead with the crest.

The Former Identities archive now sits in the open instead of behind a collapsed toggle, all several dozen punitive rebrands of it. One footnote for the historians: points totals before 2023 are approximate — the early feeds kept score like the early league kept promises. The wins are exact. Argue accordingly.

description: The old footer was four thin columns of links, two of which went to the same page, sitting next to a champion banner that only TheLeague ever saw. On AFL and Best Ball the layout quietly collapsed into a 300-pixel gutter and left half the footer empty. Nobody complained, because nobody scrolls down to be disappointed. Still. It was there, on every page, being wrong.

Now the bottom of every page opens with the champions. Full banner art, the trophy badges that team actually won, and a ribbon that counts: two titles is The Double, three is The Treble. The ribbon is per team, not per league, so in a split season the club that took the championship and its division still gets its Double while a rival holds the Premier League on the card next door. Consolation hardware does not count toward a sweep, which the NIT winner is welcome to take up with the beat desk — and neither does a conference title on a card that already has the AFL Championship, because you do not reach the title game without winning your conference.

Underneath, the same five columns on both leagues — My Team, This Week, Front Office, Record Book, League Office — so the footer stops being a different shape depending on where you are. And a Deep Cuts line surfaces the quiet corners of the site by rule: any public page the columns do not already link, chosen automatically, so the Asset Browser and the Design System stop being things only three people know the URL for. There is a Trophy Case link too, for when one banner is not enough.

Combined with the live roster feed that landed alongside this — moves hit the page within about a minute of happening on MFL — the board finally answers the only question that matters: who can I add, right now?

description: This week's 19 bug fixes and polish improvements touched the following areas of the site:

Schefter Report — Schefter's Cut Watch column got its facts straight about the August auto-cut. Sunday's article claimed the system cuts your weakest players when you skip filing a cutdown plan — flat wrong, and dangerously reassuring if your roster is loaded with recent pickups. The real rule: the machine cuts your NEWEST waiver, free-agent, and auction adds first, value be damned, and trades don't count as pickups. The shipped article was corrected, and future Cut Watch fact sheets now compute each team's actual auto-cut order with the exact code the deadline job runs — so when Schefter says the machine is coming for your quarterback, believe him. Schefter's daily Cut Watch dispatches were going straight to the website and skipping the group chat entirely — he'd type up 'Midwestside Connection faces the guillotine, 6 over the limit' for the site feed and then just... not hit send on GroupMe. Turns out the article pipeline only pings the chat for story types that define a promo, and Cut Watch never got one. Fixed: whenever at least one team is over the 22-man limit, the chat now gets the headline stat, how many players the league still needs to shed, the countdown to the August cutdown deadline, and a link to the full chopping block. On days when everyone's compliant, he keeps it to himself — no buzz for a non-story. And while we were in there, his editor dialed the column back from daily to a proper Sunday feature: one Cut Watch every Sunday morning of the cut window instead of thirty-three straight days of guillotine coverage. He also got a new source inside the league office: Schefter now knows which over-limit owners have already filed their auto-cut plans — those teams get a respectful nod for having their affairs in order, while the heat goes straight to anyone over the limit with nothing on file. He knows THAT you've made your picks, never WHICH picks — your cut list stays sealed. His chopping-block picks got smarter too: instead of just pointing at the cheapest contracts, likely cuts now come from a combined value ranking that blends redraft and dynasty ADP by contract length — a 1-year rental is judged purely on this season's draft boards, a 5-year keeper purely on dynasty boards.
